A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

+I started by standing at the east gate, wondering whether to wait or walk. The pilot data shows 160 boardings in week A and 240 in week B [@lyra:1]. These figures count trips, not unique people, so they do not indicate how many distinct students used the service [@lyra:1]. Additionally, no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1]. Because the academic schedules differed between weeks and the pilot was not randomized, the data cannot distinguish between increased ridership and changes in attendance [@lyra:1].

-My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

+The survey data compounds these limitations. Only eighteen voluntary responses were collected, exclusively from existing shuttle riders [@lyra:2]. Because non-riders were not surveyed, the results describe the preferences of the people already on the bus, not the potential demand of students who walk, bike, or take other transit [@lyra:2]. Without input from those who did not use the service, the responses cannot establish whether the shuttle met broader campus needs or simply appealed to a self-selected group of users [@lyra:2].

+That gap argues against deciding now. I recommend extending the pilot for one term, not as an endorsement of its success, but as a necessary pause to resolve the measurement problem before making a final judgment. The current evidence supports continuation only insofar as it provides the time to address the non-rider deficit. We cannot extrapolate from eighteen voluntary riders to the campus population [@lyra:2]. Therefore, the extension serves a specific investigative purpose: it allows us to design and implement a survey that reaches students who do not use the shuttle. Without this additional data, any decision about the service's future would rest on incomplete information regarding actual demand.

+The non-rider data gap identified in the Evidence section requires specific action during the extension. We must survey students who do not currently ride to determine why they avoid the service, addressing the limitation that the previous sample excluded non-riders [@lyra:2]. Additionally, we must verify whether the shuttle’s schedule aligns with actual class times, since no attendance data were collected during the initial pilot [@lyra:1]. Linking rider usage to class attendance will help determine if the service affects presence or merely facilitates trips. This targeted approach ensures the next term yields actionable evidence rather than just more anecdotal reports from those already on board.

## Evidence

I started by standing at the east gate, wondering whether to wait or walk. The pilot data shows 160 boardings in week A and 240 in week B [@lyra:1]. These figures count trips, not unique people, so they do not indicate how many distinct students used the service [@lyra:1]. Additionally, no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1]. Because the academic schedules differed between weeks and the pilot was not randomized, the data cannot distinguish between increased ridership and changes in attendance [@lyra:1].

The survey data compounds these limitations. Only eighteen voluntary responses were collected, exclusively from existing shuttle riders [@lyra:2]. Because non-riders were not surveyed, the results describe the preferences of the people already on the bus, not the potential demand of students who walk, bike, or take other transit [@lyra:2]. Without input from those who did not use the service, the responses cannot establish whether the shuttle met broader campus needs or simply appealed to a self-selected group of users [@lyra:2].

## Recommendation

That gap argues against deciding now. I recommend extending the pilot for one term, not as an endorsement of its success, but as a necessary pause to resolve the measurement problem before making a final judgment. The current evidence supports continuation only insofar as it provides the time to address the non-rider deficit. We cannot extrapolate from eighteen voluntary riders to the campus population [@lyra:2]. Therefore, the extension serves a specific investigative purpose: it allows us to design and implement a survey that reaches students who do not use the shuttle. Without this additional data, any decision about the service's future would rest on incomplete information regarding actual demand.

The non-rider data gap identified in the Evidence section requires specific action during the extension. We must survey students who do not currently ride to determine why they avoid the service, addressing the limitation that the previous sample excluded non-riders [@lyra:2]. Additionally, we must verify whether the shuttle’s schedule aligns with actual class times, since no attendance data were collected during the initial pilot [@lyra:1]. Linking rider usage to class attendance will help determine if the service affects presence or merely facilitates trips. This targeted approach ensures the next term yields actionable evidence rather than just more anecdotal reports from those already on board.

live_draft_blocks.content: The survey data compounds these limitations. Only eighteen voluntary responses were collected, exclusively from existing shuttle riders [@lyra:2]. Because non-riders were not surveyed, the results describe the preferences of the people already on the bus, not the potential demand of students who walk, bike, or take other transit [@lyra:2]. Without input from those who did not use the service, the responses cannot establish whether the shuttle met broader campus needs or simply appealed to a self-selected group of users [@lyra:2].

live_draft_blocks.heading: Recommendation
live_draft_blocks.content: That gap argues against deciding now. I recommend extending the pilot for one term, not as an endorsement of its success, but as a necessary pause to resolve the measurement problem before making a final judgment. The current evidence supports continuation only insofar as it provides the time to address the non-rider deficit. We cannot extrapolate from eighteen voluntary riders to the campus population [@lyra:2]. Therefore, the extension serves a specific investigative purpose: it allows us to design and implement a survey that reaches students who do not use the shuttle. Without this additional data, any decision about the service's future would rest on incomplete information regarding actual demand.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Recommendation
live_draft_blocks.content: The non-rider data gap identified in the Evidence section requires specific action during the extension. We must survey students who do not currently ride to determine why they avoid the service, addressing the limitation that the previous sample excluded non-riders [@lyra:2]. Additionally, we must verify whether the shuttle’s schedule aligns with actual class times, since no attendance data were collected during the initial pilot [@lyra:1]. Linking rider usage to class attendance will help determine if the service affects presence or merely facilitates trips. This targeted approach ensures the next term yields actionable evidence rather than just more anecdotal reports from those already on board.
